<reason>A controlled framing (default vs. exception, the ratchet, concession-capture) and had the more quotable lines, but B won the mechanics after Pressure Questions. B answered both questions directly and concretely (named a floor: neighborhood parks, off-peak hours, shore passage; defended fees over rules via the weekend-working nurse who can't book at dawn and via the fact that rules raise no revenue). A's answers leaned on re-assertion: "ruin is a budget choice" never met B's stipulated shortfall, and A merely repeated that concessions/permits/parking suffice after B argued they don't carry a doubled load. B neutralized A's equity core twice — "exclusion by time and luck" and "a full lot, a locked restroom, and a reservation she never gets" work by exclusion too — and defused "a price works only by being unaffordable" with waivers/free hours; A's counter that a waivered charge "raises almost nothing" was a logical slip. B also exposed the instability of A's floor/tools split (scalable parking and reservations shove overflow onto the last free surface), which A never answered. A's closing claim that B had conceded the motion was crisply dismantled in B5: the surviving difference — peak pricing of the signature asset itself — is exactly the motion's fault line. Minor execution cost to A for two nonexistent [C…] reference ids. B's "enclosure by ruin" route survived unrebutted to the end.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's parry sequence on the nurse: B2's "exclusion by time and luck" and B4's waiver/free-hours answer flipped A's strongest weapon ("a price works only by being unaffordable to someone"), and B5 then closed the loop by showing A's "you conceded the motion" victory lap ignored the one live dispute — whether the gate on the scarce signature asset may scale with demand.</best_rebuttal>
